frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d4: Six days after his first report, special representative Joseph Davies wrote again to President Roosevelt and the Secretary of State, on May 27, 1943. The second account, Document 4 of the Cairo and Tehran volume, continues his Moscow mission reporting. Davies had gone to the Soviet capital as Roosevelt's personal envoy. The record names the parties and the date only, leaving the substance of his news to the document's own pages.
frus-1944-quebec-d4:
President Roosevelt replied to Prime Minister Churchill on March 22, 1944, completing a four-day exchange of four messages. The State Department printed the whole run in the Quebec 1944 volume's opening section.

Such rapid exchanges usually meant a decision that could not wait for a meeting. In March 1944 the invasion of France was eleven weeks away, and the two governments were aligning strategy, command, and politics for it. For readers, this fourth message closes the volume's first conversation and shows the pattern of the whole file: two leaders governing a coalition by letter because events would not wait.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d4: Marshal Stalin replied to President Roosevelt on 22 July 1944, in a message preserved as document 4 of this volume. It belongs to the Foreign Relations of the United States record of the Malta and Yalta conferences, published by the Department of State. Direct letters between the two leaders carried the alliance's hardest business, and this one dates from the summer before Yalta.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d4:
Churchill forwarded a draft message to Stalin in this telegram to Truman of May 11, 1945. The Polish deadlock, the draft says, can probably now be resolved only at a conference of the three heads of government. It should sit in some unshattered town in Germany, if such can be found, at the beginning of July at the latest.

The Polish problem, the draft argues, may be easier to settle among the numerous other grave questions needing settlement with the Russians. Then the tone darkens. Churchill writes that he fears terrible things have happened during the Russian advance through Germany to the Elbe. The extract breaks off there, its warning plain.
tob-0038-d4:
Book IV completes the supplementary detailed staff reports of the Church Committee, the Senate inquiry that reported in 1976. With Book III, it forms the evidence base of the whole investigation. The committee's staff wrote these studies from agency files and sworn testimony.

Further programs and cases get the full treatment here: more on covert operations, intelligence budgets, and the handling of dissent at home. The detail is dry at times, but it is the fine print of a landmark inquiry. Researchers mining the record of 1970s intelligence reform still work through these volumes.
tob-0039-d4:
A middle roll of the Doctors' Trial transcript, Roll 5 preserves part of the 1946 to 1947 Nuremberg proceedings against Nazi medical men. The tribunal heard the case in the same courthouse as the great trial of the Nazi leaders. Its record was filmed for the archive.

Prosecution and defense contest experiments, euthanasia killings, and the chain of orders behind them, exhibit by exhibit. The transcript's dry form, with speakers named and documents numbered, is itself the point. Students of the trial, of medical ethics, and of international law draw on these rolls when they need the judgment's raw material rather than its retelling.
podcast-tuckercarlson-G-4tNK6dfD4:
Activist Charlie Kirk sits down with Tucker Carlson to talk about debt, youth anger, and party politics. Kirk leads a large conservative youth movement in the United States. The title frames his core claim about generational blame.

Kirk says heavy student and household debt has pushed young voters toward sharper politics. The talk also ranges over the Russia probe and media trust. Carlson presses him on why older leaders missed the shift. The episode gives a clear window into Kirk's pitch to young conservatives. The result is part policy talk and part campaign pitch.
podcast-joerogan-OMxdrALf8D4:
Former fighter Josh Thompson and famed referee Big John McCarthy headline Rogan's MMA Show number 179. McCarthy helped write the sport's unified rules. Thompson fought at top levels for years.

Rogan draws on both men for a deep rules and history talk. They recall how the sport grew from outlaw shows to arenas. Fights, calls, and judging errors get close review. The episode is a fight nerd's delight: two men who shaped the cage from inside it, explaining how the modern sport was built. Their bond with Rogan runs deep and shows.
frus-1945-50-intel-d4:
Stone, the Budget Bureau's assistant director for administrative management, wrote to the bureau's director, Harold Smith, on 27 August 1945. The subject area of the volume at this point is the fate of wartime intelligence. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Management experts at the Budget Bureau judged agency plans by charts, costs, and lines of command. Stone's paper brings that cold eye to the hot question of a peacetime spy service. Readers should note how early the bureau fixed its grip on the debate. Presidents listened to their budget directors, and Truman was no exception. So memos like this one helped narrow the choices long before any law was written.
frus-1861-d4:
Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote on 24 April 1861 to the American ministers in eight lands at once. The list runs from Great Britain and France to Russia, Prussia, Austria, Belgium, Italy, and Denmark. The letter is document 4 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Shots at Fort Sumter had opened the Civil War twelve days earlier. Seward now had to tell each court the same hard thing in the same words. A joint letter like this one kept the Union's case even across Europe while the fighting began. The same text to eight courts kept any one envoy from softening the Union's terms.
frus-1862-d4:
Guidance for Charles Francis Adams left Washington on 13 December 1861, signed by William H. Seward. The printed record keeps it as Document 4 in the 1862 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs volume. By then, in the close of the war's first year, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

Outbound letters like this one told the envoy what line to take and what to report back. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1863p1-d4:
On 15 November 1862, Charles Francis Adams wrote from London to Secretary of State William H. Seward. Adams served as the American minister to Britain. The dispatch is document 4 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Adams wrote in a season of strain. The South's friends in Britain pushed for their cause to be backed, while the North's blockade bit harder each month. His letters weighed each move in Parliament and the press for signs of a shift. This one adds its share to a record that still reads as the day book of the war's most watched legation.
